article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: CMP active, collaborative pedagogy with productive struggle and productive persistence in the corequisite pairs
description: The instructional design carried from the original Quantway and Statway pathways into the new corequisite courses: student-centered, collaborative problem solving in authentic contexts, small-group productive struggle, and productive persistence supports for mindset and belonging. The report states that "the pedagogy centers on active, collaborative learning within rich, authentic contexts," using themes such as citizenship, personal finance, medical literacy, and social justice. Both the college-level course and the developmental-level corequisite use this pedagogy. Faculty reported initial student resistance to struggling in groups with minimal instructor support, followed by deeper engagement once students adapted, and noted that time pressure sometimes pushed them back toward direct instruction.
requirements: Faculty preparation time or prior experience with CMP curricula to build familiarity with the pedagogy and materials
constraints: Under time constraints, faculty reduced time for collaboration, exploration, and discovery and used more direct instruction, selecting which rich tasks students could fully explore
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics
target_learning_goals: Engagement, persistence, and deep learning of quantitative reasoning or statistics concepts
examples: Faculty observed that social-emotional supports helped develop students' persistence and nurtured a sense of community and belonging in the classroom
key_sources: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: Cross-modal transformer (CMT) module aligning performance audio with symbolic score features
description: The Cross-Modal Transformer is the feature-alignment core of the model, chosen over simple concatenation or additive attention because it "dynamically captures cross-modal correlations via the cross-attention mechanism". Audio is represented with MFCC features at a 44,100 Hz sampling rate and the score modality uses 512-dimensional word embeddings; both are fused in a 1,024-dimensional CMT architecture (6 layers, 8 attention heads, ~48M parameters) trained with a contrastive loss using cosine similarity, batch size N and temperature τ = 0.07. The module outputs aligned feature vectors that feed both the big data analysis module and the generative AI module.
requirements: Synchronous PCM audio input and digitized score text in Event Encoding Sequence Format
Pre-training of the CMT feature extraction layers (on MAESTRO v3.0.0) before the layers are frozen for deployment
constraints: CQT was computed only for auxiliary visualization and was not provided to the model; all reported performance metrics reflect MFCC-based processing only
Piano and guitar practice excerpts were restricted to monophonic melodic lines to maintain compatibility with the audio processing pipeline
target_learners: undergraduate music majors learning piano, violin, flute or guitar
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of pitch, rhythm and expressive deviations in student performance
examples: The architecture configuration fixed 6 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden dimension 1,024, dropout 0.1, and sinusoidal positional encoding across all experiments
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: Can we further improve tablet-based drawing to enhance learning? An empirical test of two types of support
citation: Steffen P. Schmidgall, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Can we further improve tablet-based drawing to enhance learning? An empirical test of two types of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09513-6
title: Cognitive Model of Drawing Construction (CMDC)
description: The CMDC, due to Van Meter and Firetto (2013) as described in this article, explains representational drawing when learning from text as "a set of interleaved perceptual and cognitive processes that contribute to the construction of an internal mental model of the text which is then externalized in a drawing". The drawing externalizes the mental model and provides feedback about the coherence and completeness of learners' mental models, which can be improved by reviewing the text contents. The model is based on models of learning with multiple representations such as the integrated model of text and picture comprehension. It predicts that beneficial effects of drawing appear only if the type of assessment is matched to the type of mental model constructed through the drawing activity, i.e., higher-order rather than lower-order knowledge.
requirements: Learners must actively reconsider and evaluate their drawings for the feedback function of the externalized drawing to improve mental model construction.
constraints: The article states benefits appear only when the type of assessment matches the type of mental model constructed through the drawing activity.
target_learners: university students learning expository science text
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension and transfer of visuo-spatial science content
examples: The study tested the CMDC-aligned prediction that drawing benefits higher-order measures (transfer, drawing test) but not recognition.
key_sources: Steffen P. Schmidgall, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Can we further improve tablet-based drawing to enhance learning? An empirical test of two types of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09513-6

article_title: Correlates of teachers’ classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Duan, S., Bissaker, K., & Xu, Z. (2024). Correlates of teachers' classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09881-2
title: Three-strand conceptual framework of CMSE correlates: teacher-level, classroom-level, and school-level factors
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework, adapted from Fackler et al.'s three categories of TSE-related factors, that organizes correlates of classroom management self-efficacy into three strands: "(1) personal characteristics of teacher (teacher-level factors); (2) characteristics of classroom composition (classroom-level factors); (3) teachers' working conditions (school-level factors)". The framework, presented in Fig. 1, guided both the synthesis of the literature and the discussion of areas needing further exploration.
requirements: Correlates must be empirically tested in studies measuring teacher self-efficacy for classroom management with quantifiable relationships
constraints: The framework captures correlates that are both theoretically and empirically tested, per the article
target_learners: in-service teachers in mainstream school settings
examples: The meta-analysis used the framework to cluster 22 identified correlates into the three categories and to structure the discussion of results
key_sources: Duan, S., Bissaker, K., & Xu, Z. (2024). Correlates of teachers' classroom management self-efficacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09881-2

article_title: Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers’ Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0
title: Two-part model linking classroom management scripts to situational awareness, mode of cognition, and event representation
description: The second part of the model depicts how activated classroom management scripts influence teachers' visual perception, situational awareness, mode of cognition, and event representation. It draws on Endsley's theory of situational awareness, whose "three levels" are perception, comprehension, and projection, and on Eraut's theory of workplace learning for mode of cognition. The model presumes novices become overloaded in perceiving, understanding, and responding, while experts' scripts guide perceptual attention efficiently, equating integrated situational awareness with withitness.
requirements: Situational awareness is tightly coupled with mode of cognition; perception and event representation interact in a recurring loop of input and interpretation
constraints: The model itself is not entirely linear, as indicated by the arrows in the model
target_learners: pre-service and novice teachers
teacher educators
examples: The model is presented in Fig. 3 contrasting novices' continual image-driven scanning and prolonged analysis with experts' automatic scanning and pattern recognition
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0

article_title: The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis
citation: Lin, H. (2012). The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis. In L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds.), CALL: Using, Learning, Knowing, EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://research-publishing.net
title: Six-variable moderator framework for the effectiveness of CMC in SLA
description: The article organizes its meta-analysis around substantive and methodological features that may condition how effective CMC interventions are for L2 learning. Twelve study-level features were coded for each of the 56 studies, and the results section states that "task type, group size, participants' educational level, CMC mode, CMC tool and outcome measures were potential moderators that would affect the overall effectiveness of CMC intervention". The framework treats CMC effectiveness not as fixed but as contingent on instructional and methodological design choices, guiding how future CMC studies and implementations should be described and compared.
requirements: Primary studies must report adequate quantitative information for effect sizes to be calculated, and each study must use some form of CMC either exclusively or with other instructional tools.
constraints: Detailed moderator analysis results were not included in the paper due to space limitations, so the framework's moderator effects are reported as tentative findings without magnitudes.
Eligible studies were limited to those published between 2000 and 2011 with L2 or foreign language learners and experimental or quasi-experimental designs.
target_learners: L2 and foreign language learners in middle school, primary school, and university/college settings
target_learning_goals: Second/foreign language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing
examples: The meta-analysis coded 56 primary studies at two levels — study-feature coding and effect-size coding — reaching a final inter-rater reliability of 98%.
key_sources: Lin, H. (2012). The Effectiveness of Computer-Mediated Communication on SLA: A Meta-Analysis and Research Synthesis. In L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds.), CALL: Using, Learning, Knowing, EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. Research-publishing.net. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574920

article_title: Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum
citation: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL.
title: Set of 415 revisions to visuals in the 7th-grade CMP2 curriculum
description: The research team revised visuals in the Connected Mathematics 2 seventh-grade curriculum as part of a randomized controlled trial. Table 2 reports "The total number of revisions was 415 across 397 instances," with 69% being whole-visual removals of decorative or representational illustrations, 3% added mathematically-relevant visuals, and the remainder text-visual integration moves and modifications within existing visuals such as labels and color coding. Table 1 shows 47% of the original 432 visuals were math-irrelevant.
requirements: Revisions were guided by the multimedia, signaling, contiguity, and coherence principles and implemented by the research team
constraints: The article notes the math-relevant visuals were already well designed, so revisions focused mostly on removing math-irrelevant visuals and improving integration
target_learners: 7th-grade mathematics students
examples: Examples in the appendix include adding a labelled diagram (multimedia), color coding (signaling), moving a table onto the same page as its problems (contiguity), and removing decorative or representational visuals (coherence)
key_sources: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574965

article_title: Effects of the Connected Mathematics Project 2 (CMP2) on the Mathematics Achievement of Grade 6 Students in the Mid-Atlantic Region. Final Report. NCEE 2012-4017
citation: Martin, T., Brasiel, S. J., Turner, H., & Wise, J. C. (2012). Effects of the Connected Mathematics Project 2 (CMP2) on the Mathematics Achievement of Grade 6 Students in the Mid-Atlantic Region (NCEE 2012-4017). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: CMP2 curriculum and professional development package
description: Connected Mathematics Project 2 is a problem-centered mathematics curriculum for grades 6–8 in which "students progress through a series of units made up of problem-centered investigations that address core mathematics topics." Students are introduced to a problem, work in groups to develop solution strategies, and justify their thinking by presenting solutions to the class, with practice problem sets in each investigation. The accompanying teacher PD is "intended to deepen teacher understanding of mathematics, strengthen their pedagogical knowledge, and develop their ability to use inquiry-based instructional strategies." In the study it was provided with all standard publisher PD and materials.
requirements: Teachers receive the standard publisher professional development, including training days before and during the school year
Implementation per publisher recommendations: 50 minutes of class time per day and six units per school year
constraints: The study states impacts reflect assignment to use CMP2, not necessarily of actually using CMP2, because the study team did not ensure a particular amount or quality of instruction
target_learners: Grade 6 students (curriculum designed for grades 6–8)
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and procedural skills in mathematics
examples: In the evaluation, intervention teachers received two days of PD before the school year and three days during the implementation year, plus standard curriculum materials for both study years
key_sources: Martin, T., Brasiel, S. J., Turner, H., & Wise, J. C. (2012). Effects of the Connected Mathematics Project 2 (CMP2) on the Mathematics Achievement of Grade 6 Students in the Mid-Atlantic Region (NCEE 2012-4017). article_title: Effects of the Connected Mathematics Project 2 (CMP2) on the Mathematics Achievement of Grade 6 Students in the Mid-Atlantic Region. Final Report. NCEE 2012-4017
citation: Martin, T., Brasiel, S. J., Turner, H., & Wise, J. C. (2012). Effects of the Connected Mathematics Project 2 (CMP2) on the Mathematics Achievement of Grade 6 Students in the Mid-Atlantic Region (NCEE 2012-4017). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: CMP2 inquiry-based instructional model of active, collaborative student learning
description: CMP2 embodies an instructional model in which "CMP2 allows students to be responsible for their learning by exploring different solution pathways, sharing their ideas with other students, listening to the ideas of others, and questioning each other." Teachers ensure lesson goals are met by asking questions, encouraging students to share and compare their thinking, and connect representations of problems and solutions. The report identifies four elements of effective mathematics instruction it incorporates: active student participation in building knowledge, motivation and engagement through contexts connected to student experience, collaborative learning through group problem solving, and development of conceptual understanding and procedural knowledge.
requirements: Teachers act as facilitators who introduce problems, circulate during open work periods, and connect presentations to prior learning and core mathematical concepts
constraints: Some researchers question such inquiry methods, arguing that they could place a high demand on working memory, as the report notes in its review of the research base
target_learners: Middle school students in grades 6–8
Grade 6 students in the Mid-Atlantic region
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of core mathematics topics
Student responsibility for learning and complex thinking
examples: Each investigation follows the sequence: problem introduction, group work to share ideas and develop strategies, presentation of solution strategies to the class, and practice problem sets

article_title: Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students
citation: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17
title: Six-phase lesson sequence for contextual mathematical thinking
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern with six ordered syntax steps: (1) presentation of contextual problems; (2) asking critical and analytical questions; (3) individual and group investigation; (4) presentation and discussion; (5) reflection; and (6) a higher-order thinking test. Each step has specified teacher and student activities and an allocated time, moving from lower-order questions that "lead to a higher-order thinking questions" and from individual problem-solving to group discussion and public presentation.
requirements: Contextual problems presented via pictures, stories or videos that enable critical, analytical and creative thinking
Worksheets for individual investigation followed by group discussion
Time allocations per step as set out in the syntax table
constraints: Designed and tested for middle school mathematics (Grade VIII geometry topics)
target_learners: Grade VIII junior high school students
examples: Table 2 details each phase: e.g. the investigation phase gives students worksheets, asks them to solve problems independently, then join groups while the teacher provides scaffolding
key_sources: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17

article_title: Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students
citation: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17
title: Combine contextual problems, critical questioning, investigation, discussion, reflection and testing to support higher-order thinking
description: The article argues the model supports higher-order thinking completely because each phase contributes a distinct support: varied contextual problems, analytical and critical questioning, individual and group work, public presentation, and reflection plus testing. It states the model "provides support for the development of higher-order thinking ability completely", with each component mutually supporting the others toward the intended purpose.
requirements: All six syntax phases are passed as a whole process; the article says the steps "have been prepared with a logical flow that must be passed as a whole process"
constraints: Effectiveness evidence is limited to the reported 78-student implementation
target_learners: Grade VIII junior high school students
target_learning_goals: reasoning, critical and creative abilities; higher-order thinking ability
examples: In the discussion the authors map each phase to a support: questioning supports openness of thinking, group work supports collaborative thinking, presentation strengthens confidence to defend ideas
key_sources: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17

article_title: A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan
citation: Muhammad U. Farooq, AbdulRahman Al Asmari & Choudhary Z. Javid. (2012). A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p91
title: The CMC-ELT Blended Learning Model
description: The CMC-ELT Blended Learning Model is a need-oriented framework that enhances previous distance education models "by adding the component of technology with distance education to create a more cost-efficient way of bringing the learning environment to the learners". It adopts a collaborative constructivist perspective associated with Dewey's principles of interaction and continuity, and uses text-based communication as its primary mode. The model was implemented through AIOU's Olive virtual learning environment, built in Moodle, providing tools for tutors to present materials and mark assignments, for students to manage progress and communicate, and for administration to produce reports.
requirements: Implementation within a general distance educational setting, taking into account the nature of the programme, the subject matter, the profile of the students, the support facilities and educational technology available
constraints: The model "does not project a new pedagogical framework but it enhances the previous models of learning"
target_learners: Post-graduate MA TEFL students in distance education
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and self-directed learning abilities
examples: The model was implemented with 27 randomly selected MA TEFL students at AIOU through the Olive VLS, including online study material, tutorials, assignment submission and tutor feedback.
key_sources: Muhammad U. Farooq, AbdulRahman Al Asmari & Choudhary Z. Javid. (2012). A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p91

article_title: Integrating Cognitive-Motivational Strategies into Multimedia-Based English Instruction for Low-Achievers
citation: Chang, M. M., & Lin, M.-C. (2012). Integrating cognitive-motivational strategies into multimedia-based English instruction for low-achievers. In L. Bradley & S. title: Cognitive-motivational multimedia CALL model (CMMCALL)
description: The CMMCALL is an interactive multimedia CALL model that combines motivational and cognitive strategy elements to guide instructional design for language learning. The article states it "consists of elements including attention, relevance (motivational aspect) and selecting and integrating (cognitive aspect)" and was "constructed with the integration of cognitive-motivational CALL model (CMMCALL) ... according to language learning theories and the findings from the literature review." The model draws on Keller's ARCS motivation model and strategy instruction research.
requirements: Multimedia environment must allow students to choose learning time and control pace and sequencing of instructional events
constraints: Validated with a small sample of English majors and non-majors before the main study
target_learners: low-achieving college English learners
examples: A sample page of the CMMCALL program is shown in Figure 1 of the article

article_title: Latent profiles of grit, self-control, belonging, and college motives: differential effects of self-control on academic performance among Chilean university students.
citation: Tornero Bernardita, Cárcamo Marcela, Rengifo Manuel, Tricio Jorge, A. Rojas-Barahona Cristian, Gaete Jorge. (2026). Latent profiles of grit, self-control, belonging, and college motives: differential effects of self-control on academic performance among Chilean university students. BMC Psychology, 14, 937. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04650-y
title: Conceptual Utility Model for the Management of Stress and Psychological Wellbeing (CMMSPW™)
description: The CMMSPW™ is an integrative framework organizing psychological and contextual variables into presage, process, and product factors, building on the Presage–Process–Product (3P) framework. The article states it "organizes psychological and contextual variables into a structured system of predictive, mediating, and outcome factors". In this study, grit, self-control, belonging, and motives are treated as process variables and standardized first-year GPA as the product variable, with self-control framed as a core regulatory mechanism within the process domain.
requirements: Requires measurement of presage variables (demographics, prior achievement), process variables (motivational and socio-cognitive constructs), and product variables (academic performance, well-being)
constraints: The article notes contextual variables such as institutional support, teaching practices, or family educational background were not fully captured in the present study's focus on individual psychological characteristics
target_learners: university students
examples: The study situated grit, self-control, sense of belonging, and college motives as process variables and standardized first-year GPA as the product variable within the framework
key_sources: Tornero Bernardita, Cárcamo Marcela, Rengifo Manuel, Tricio Jorge, A. Rojas-Barahona Cristian, Gaete Jorge. (2026). Latent profiles of grit, self-control, belonging, and college motives: differential effects of self-control on academic performance among Chilean university students. article_title: Combination of mentor-based and resident-based learning may benefit to improving the ability of clinical practice in resident training.
citation: Li Min, Liu Tao, Wen Yiqiong, Zhang Min, Zhu Wenye, Wang Xuming, Hou Yunjiao, Li Lin, Zu Anju, Sun Shibo. (2025). Combination of mentor-based and resident-based learning may benefit to improving the ability of clinical practice in resident training. BMC Medical Education 25:197. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06798-4
title: CMRL: a combined mentor-based and resident-based learning mode with a 4:1 mentor-to-trainee time ratio
description: CMRL is a complementary learning mode the authors proposed for standardized resident training, in which "senior doctors as SRT mentors guiding the trainees combines with the trainees engaging in medical activities independently to help trainees acquire clinical knowledge and skills through bedside teaching." In the trial it was implemented as four mentor-dominated days plus one trainee-dominated day per week for four weeks, with the mentor supervising and making remedial medical activities only when patient safety was threatened. Assessment used objective ratios of trainee to mentor diagnoses, disposals, and medical orders.
requirements: Mentors uniformly trained to the same guidance and evaluation standards before the study
Mentor supervision with remedial medical activities during trainee-dominated time to ensure patient safety
constraints: The study failed to investigate whether further increasing the time dominated by trainees would be more beneficial
Single-center study with a small sample size; non-blinded RCT
target_learners: second-year junior residents in standardized residency training
target_learning_goals: clinical practice ability including diagnosis, comprehensive analysis, prescribing medical orders, communication skills, and patient care
examples: In the RCT, the CMRL group spent four days per week in mentor-led activities and one day per week performing medical activities independently while the mentor observed and intervened only for patient safety
key_sources: Li Min, Liu Tao, Wen Yiqiong, Zhang Min, Zhu Wenye, Wang Xuming, Hou Yunjiao, Li Lin, Zu Anju, Sun Shibo. (2025). Combination of mentor-based and resident-based learning may benefit to improving the ability of clinical practice in resident training. BMC Medical Education 25:197. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06798-4

article_title: Teaching conflict management to medical students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Mohseni Fatemeh, Mohammadi Aeen, Khabaz Mafinejad Mahboobeh, Khajavirad Nasim, Basiri Kamal, Gruppen Larry D. (2024). Teaching conflict management to medical students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06514-8
title: Conflict Management Attitude questionnaire (CMAQ)
description: The CMAQ is a 12-item self-report questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale measuring attitudes toward conflict management, with three subscales: Perceived Interactions in Conflict Management (four items), Perceived Value of Learning Conflict Management (five items), and Perceived Application of Conflict Management (three items). The article reports "Cronbach's alpha coefficient for 12 items of the questionnaire was 0.791", with all items above CVI 0.88 and CVR 0.75. It served as the pre- and post-test outcome measure in this trial.
requirements: Administration before and after the intervention via self-report (here, Google Form)
constraints: Self-reported attitudes, so the authors note self-enhancement could have created a bias
target_learners: medical students
examples: Used at the beginning and end of the last (fourth) week in both trial groups
key_sources: Mohseni Fatemeh, Mohammadi Aeen, Khabaz Mafinejad Mahboobeh, Khajavirad Nasim, Basiri Kamal, Gruppen Larry D. (2024). Teaching conflict management to medical students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06514-8

article_title: Randomized controlled trial of the CMR immersive virtual reality (IVR) headset training compared to e-learning for operating room configuration of the CMR versius robot.
citation: Eley Catherine L., Palaniappan Varun, Carter Abbie, Sogaolu Opeyemi, Horwood James, Davies Michael, Torkington Jared, Ansell James. (2024). Randomized controlled trial of the CMR immersive virtual reality (IVR) headset training compared to e-learning for operating room configuration of the CMR versius robot. Journal of Robotic Surgery 18(1):143. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-01885-y
title: CMR Versius immersive virtual reality headset training modules for operating room set-up
description: A set of six VR headset modules for the CMR Versius robotic platform that let participants "complete 'learn mode' and subsequently 'practice mode' for each of the 6 modules to set up the robotic system in a simulated virtual reality operating room environment". Modules cover surgeon console preparation, connecting bedside units, draping, instrument identification and attachment, port training, and entering surgical mode. Unlike most surgical simulators, they focus on system set-up rather than surgical technique, using the platform's open console and modular design.
requirements: Participants need access to the IVR headset and individualized Versius Connect portal log in details; the trial allotted a two-week completion period.
constraints: The article states the VR Headset is a new addition but not yet a compulsory component of the CMR learning pathway, and its face and content validity had yet to be established.
target_learners: Robot-naive medical students
Theatre staff and surgeons learning robotic system set-up
target_learning_goals: Operating room configuration of the CMR Versius robotic system
examples: In the trial, the intervention group completed learn and practice mode for the 6 VR modules over two weeks before a blinded live set-up assessment.
